name: lightweight-entity
intent: Keep domain entity classes free of persistence logic - no queries, no save/delete, no table knowledge - so that all knowledge of how the object maps to the store lives in metadata (annotations, mapping files, tags, descriptor tables) that a generic mapper consumes.
problem: When each entity class carries its own mapping code (table name, column list, SQL, load/save methods) the same schema knowledge is duplicated in every class, the domain model is welded to the store, and a schema change becomes an edit inside the model. Moving the mapping out then raises the reverse problem: the entities must be dumb enough for a generic mapper to drive them, i.e. they may carry state and domain behaviour but no persistence behaviour.
context: The persistence-state layer of an application whose domain objects outlive a single operation: entities are stored relationally or document-wise, their schema evolves independently of the model, and a mapper (Data Mapper/ORM/session) - not the object itself - must own reads, writes, identity and lazy loading. It applies where the language can carry mapping metadata outside the entity (annotations, XML/DSL mapping files, struct tags, descriptor tables, external schema files) and something can read that metadata generically.
benefits: Mapping knowledge has one home: adding a column, renaming a table or retargeting a deployment becomes a metadata edit instead of an edit in every entity class, and two classes can no longer disagree about the same schema.
The domain model stays portable and testable: entities can be constructed, mutated and asserted with plain language constructs, because they never open connections, write SQL or consult a session.
Uniform cross-cutting persistence behaviour - dirty checking, versioning, auditing, cascades, lazy loading - can be implemented once in the mapper, since every entity looks alike to it.
Schema evolution and model refactoring decouple: the mapping layer absorbs legacy names, table splits and renames without touching domain behaviour.
One metadata source can serve several purposes: the same mapping can drive DDL/migrations, validation or a generated query client instead of a second hand-maintained description.
Entities compose with ordinary value objects and inheritance structures, because the mapper - not the entity - carries the knowledge of how the object shape maps to rows.
tradeoffs: An extra indirection: the mapping layer must be configured, learned and kept in sync with the database, and metadata that drifts from the schema fails at runtime rather than at compile time unless the toolchain validates or generates it.
Persistence semantics move out of the entity, so failures surface as mapper output - generated SQL, proxies, deferred loads, opaque framework errors - and debugging crosses an abstraction boundary.
Reflection- or attribute-driven mapping costs startup and per-row time unless the mapper caches the metadata or compiles the model; very short-lived entities can pay that cost on every operation.

The dumb entity invites an anaemic domain model: once behaviour and invariants are pushed into services, the object degrades into a row-shaped record and business rules scatter into transaction scripts.

Metadata is a wide binding surface - annotations, tags and schema files can bind more columns than an operation intends (mass assignment/over-posting) and pull schema vocabulary into the entity's public surface.
Defaults are inferred, not stated: conventions (table naming, key discovery, nullability) differ between tools and databases, so implicit metadata must be pinned down explicitly wherever it matters.
Lazy loading proxies add overhead on hot paths and can trigger unexpected queries when serialized across process boundaries (e.g., in distributed sessions or cached objects).
Bidirectional navigation relationships require careful management to avoid circular proxy dependencies that confuse the mapper and inflate the object graph on load.

participants.responsibility: Holds domain state and domain behaviour only; contains no connection, session, query or table knowledge and depends on no persistence API.
Declarative description of how entity fields correspond to store columns, keys and relationships - annotations, XML/DSL mapping files, struct tags, schema declarations or descriptor tables.
Reads the mapping metadata once per entity type and turns it into a runtime mapping model (column list, key columns, converters, relationships), usually with caching or code generation.
Generic engine that uses the mapping model to load, insert, update and delete instances and to keep identity consistent; entity classes never call it themselves.
Repository, unit of work or session through which application code reaches the mapper; it collects the entity's changes and decides when they are written.

use_cases: Layered applications whose domain model is persisted through an ORM: JPA/Hibernate annotations or orm.xml, EF Core configuration, SQLAlchemy mappings, Diesel/SeaORM derives.
Products that map one domain model onto different schemas per customer or deployment through interchangeable metadata sets, without recompiling the model.
Legacy schemas with hostile column names and shapes that must not leak into the domain model: the mapping layer is the translation seam.
Systems that need entities testable in isolation without a database, while the mapping layer is exercised separately against a real database.
Schema-as-code workflows where the mapping metadata also drives migrations or DDL and generated query clients (Prisma, EF Core migrations, SQLAlchemy metadata.create_all).
CQRS read-side projections: lightweight entities serve as denormalized read models populated from the write side, with no behaviour beyond data access.
Event-sourcing snapshots: entities are rebuilt from an event stream and must carry state without invoking the event store.
API boundary DTOs that translate between the internal domain model and external representations, decoupling schema evolution from API contracts.
Distributed system message payloads: serialized lightweight entities travel across process boundaries (queues, event buses) where no persistence context exists.
Hibernate/JPA applications can keep POJO entities focused on domain state while annotations or XML mapping descriptors tell the ORM how to persist them through an EntityManager or Session.

EF Core applications can configure CLR entity-to-table and property-to-column metadata in OnModelCreating/Fluent API or data annotations, leaving persistence orchestration in the DbContext rather than entity methods.
SQLAlchemy applications can use registry-based declarative or imperative mappings to bind Python classes to tables while sessions, not entities, own database operations.
avoid_when: The object is a plain row record with no behaviour (a DTO around one table): an Active Record or a table data gateway is less machinery.
Throwaway scripts and simple CRUD tools where the table is effectively the model: direct SQL or a table data gateway is simpler than maintaining a mapping layer.
The mapping is trivial (a handful of columns on one table) and no mapper exists in the stack: hand-written mapping in the gateway gives the same separation without metadata.

The entity must enforce persistence-aware invariants itself (optimistic-locking guards, audit stamps computed inside the object): a mapper-supported domain model with explicit mapping code fits better than pretending the entity is ignorant.
The store shape already matches the object graph and serialization is acceptable - see Serialized Entity instead of column mapping.
anti_patterns: Annotation spam presented as metadata mapping: dozens of framework attributes on a class that is still only a row holder, coupling the domain model to schema and framework at once.
Adding save/delete/find helpers to the 'lightweight' entity the first time a mapper call feels verbose - the class silently turns into an Active Record and mapping logic forks.
Duplicating mapping knowledge in both metadata and hand-written SQL, so the metadata is decorative and drifts from the queries that actually run.
Turning every entity into a data structure with no behaviour and no invariants, then collecting all rules in a service layer - the anaemic domain model the pattern is blamed for.
Treating generated or convention-derived mappings as the domain contract, so a database rename forces a domain rename.
Exposing entity IDs to external callers (e.g., as API resource identifiers) and later discovering that the persistence identity must change but is already baked into contracts.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: domain state and behaviour vs. persistence mapping.
Single source of truth for the schema mapping (the metadata), instead of per-class duplicates.
Persistence ignorance / dependency inversion: the entity depends on nothing persistence-specific, while the mapping layer depends on the entity's shape.
Open/closed: new entities and columns arrive as new metadata, not as edits to existing mappers.
Information hiding: generated SQL, identity and connection details stay behind the mapper/facade boundary.
Immutability by default: prefer read-only fields/properties to avoid concurrency issues with shared entity instances.
Explicit over implicit: pin all conventions that the application relies on rather than depending on framework defaults.
best_practices: Keep entities free of persistence calls; put save/find/delete on repositories or a session, never on the entity.
Declare field/column, key and converter metadata explicitly wherever conventions are not guaranteed, and pin the conventions that are relied on.
Validate metadata against the live schema at startup - or generate both from one source - so drift fails fast instead of at the first query.
Cache or compile the mapping model on hot paths and measure reflection/attribute-lookup cost before assuming it is free.
Restrict the write surface per operation (DTOs, immutable metadata, allow-lists) so the generic mapper cannot over-post columns an operation should not touch.
Test entities with plain unit tests and the mapping layer against a real or containerised database; do not let integration setup leak into domain tests.
Prefer immutable entity classes (final fields, readonly properties) where the domain permits, to eliminate thread-safety concerns and make side-effects explicit.
Separate read and write models (CQRS) when query shapes differ significantly from command shapes; do not force the write-side entity to serve read projections.

Use embeddable/value-object types for fine-grained composition within a single table row (Hibernate @Embeddable, EF Core owned types, Prisma value objects) rather than modelling everything as a top-level entity.
Profile generated SQL under realistic access patterns; lazy-loading proxies that survive serialization into caches or message payloads cause runtime failures.
Apply optimistic locking (Hibernate @Version, EF Core row-version) when concurrent modification is plausible, and let the mapper detect conflicts rather than hand-rolling checks.
sources: Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2003) - Metadata Mapping (Chapter 13, Object-Relational Metadata Mapping Patterns): mapping details held in metadata and processed by generic code; the Data Mapper discussion keeps persistence knowledge out of the domain object.
Evans, Domain-Driven Design (2004) - Entity and Value Object distinctions; the persistence-ignorance principle that keeps domain logic free of infrastructure concerns.
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/data/ef-rp/intro - ASP.NET Core Razor Pages tutorial demonstrating POCO entity development with EF Core.
